title: Atmosphere
tagline: Composition and layers of the atmosphere, insolation, pressure, winds, humidity and precipitation

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The composition and layer boundaries are the standard textbook values; the heights of the layers vary slightly with latitude and season, and the chapter says so where it matters. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: State the composition of dry air and the role of water vapour.
Name the layers of the atmosphere and give the height, the temperature trend and the main feature of each.
Explain insolation and the greenhouse effect.
Describe the pressure belts and the wind systems that lie between them.
Distinguish between humidity and precipitation and explain how rain, snow, sleet and hail form.

overview.intro: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases that surrounds the Earth. It is held to the surface by gravity and it is denser near the ground and thinner higher up. Dry air is made up of about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide, neon, hydrogen and helium in very small amounts, and with water vapour, whose share changes from almost nothing over the poles to about 4 per cent in the warm humid air over the tropics. The atmosphere is divided into layers, each with its own behaviour of temperature. In the troposphere, where we live and where all weather occurs, the temperature falls with height at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre. Above it the stratosphere holds the ozone layer, and above that the mesosphere is the coldest place in the atmosphere and the place where meteors burn up. The heat that drives the whole system comes from the Sun, and the way that heat is absorbed, trapped and transferred between the surface and the atmosphere produces pressure differences, winds, clouds and rain.

facts.label: Composition of dry air
facts.value: About 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and other gases in trace amounts

facts.label: Troposphere
facts.value: Up to about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the Equator; all weather occurs here

facts.label: Ozone layer
facts.value: In the stratosphere, it absorbs much of the harmful ultra-violet radiation from the Sun

facts.label: Temperature gradient
facts.value: Temperature falls at about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometre of height in the troposphere

learn.title: Composition and structure of the atmosphere

blocks.text: The atmosphere is thicker at the Equator than at the poles, because the greater weight of the overlying air there compresses it more, and it is denser near the ground, where the weight of the air above is greatest. Air thins with height, so the weight of the atmosphere at sea level is about 1.0 kilogram per square centimetre, that is the standard atmosphere, and it falls to almost nothing at 100 kilometres. Because the air thins, the atmosphere has no sharp upper boundary; the exosphere merges gradually into the space between the stars. The composition given for dry air excludes water vapour, whose share varies from under 1 per cent in cold air to about 4 per cent in warm, humid air.

items: The thickness of the troposphere is greatest at the Equator, where the air is warm and expanded, and least at the poles.
Temperature falls with height in the troposphere because the heat is received from below, from the surface that the Sun has warmed.
The stratosphere warms with height because ozone absorbs ultra-violet radiation and the energy is converted into heat.
The mesosphere is the coldest region of the atmosphere, and the meteor showers seen from the surface are the burning up of meteors there.
The height of the tropopause is lowest over the poles, which is why the weather of the polar regions is confined to a shallow layer.

blocks.text: Insolation is the solar energy that reaches the Earth and is absorbed by it. The amount received at any place depends on the angle at which the rays strike the surface and on the length of the day. At the Equator the rays strike directly and the days are long, so more heat is received; towards the poles the rays strike obliquely and have to pass through a longer stretch of atmosphere, so less reaches the surface. Some energy is reflected back by clouds, dust and the surface itself, and the proportion reflected is called the albedo. The rest is absorbed by the atmosphere, by the land and by the sea, and it is this absorbed energy that drives the circulation of the atmosphere and of the ocean.

items.meaning: The solar energy received by the Earth.
The proportion of the incoming solar energy that is reflected back to space.
The warming of the lower atmosphere by gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour that absorb the outgoing terrestrial radiation and send part of it back downwards.
The long-wave heat energy that the warmed surface of the Earth sends out.
The state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time.
The average weather of a place, taken over a long period of at least thirty years.

items: The greenhouse effect is natural and without it the Earth would be far colder and could not support life as we know it.
Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are the principal greenhouse gases; ozone and nitrous oxide also contribute.
The burning of fossil fuels, the destruction of forests and the increase in the concentration of methane increase the greenhouse effect, which is the main cause of the present warming of the globe.
A weather instrument that measures the intensity of insolation is a actinometer, and one that measures the radiation from the body is a pyrheliometer.
Because the Sun's rays strike obliquely at the poles, a smaller area of the Earth is heated there, so the pole receives far less insolation than the Equator.

blocks.text: Air pressure is the weight of the overlying air pressing on a unit area, so it is greatest at sea level and falls with height. A place of low pressure is one in which air is rising, and a place of high pressure is one in which air is sinking and flowing out at the surface. Wind is air moving from high pressure towards low pressure, and it is deflected by the rotation of the Earth, to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. This deflection, together with the alternation of the heated and cooled zones, produces the belt of winds in each hemisphere.

items: The trade winds blow steadily from the subtropical high towards the equatorial low, that is from the north-east in the Northern Hemisphere and from the south-east in the Southern Hemisphere.
The westerlies blow from the subpolar low towards the subtropical high, that is from the south-west in the Northern Hemisphere and from the north-west in the Southern Hemisphere.
The polar easterlies blow from the polar high towards the subpolar low.
Wind is named after the direction it comes from, so a north-westerly wind comes from the north-west.
The Coriolis force is the deflection of wind caused by the rotation of the Earth; it is zero at the Equator and strongest at the poles.

items.text: Why are the trade winds called the trade winds?
items.note: In the days of sailing ships they were the winds that carried traders reliably across the tropical oceans, and the name has been used ever since. They are steady and regular, blowing all the year from the same quarter, which is what made them so useful to the early traders.

blocks.text: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Absolute humidity is the actual amount of water vapour present in a given volume of air, while relative humidity is that amount expressed as a percentage of the maximum the air could hold at that temperature. Relative humidity falls as the air is heated, because warm air can hold more water vapour, and it reaches 100 per cent at the dew point, the temperature at which the air becomes saturated. When air is cooled below the dew point, the excess water vapour condenses on dust particles to form clouds, and when the droplets grow large enough to fall, precipitation begins. The forms of precipitation depend on the temperature of the air between the cloud and the ground.

blocks.caption: Table: forms of precipitation
rows: Drops of water that fall as liquid; the usual form in the tropics and in temperate lands in summer
Falls as ice crystals when the temperature remains below freezing all the way down
Rain that freezes on passing through a shallow layer of freezing air near the ground
Balls of ice that grow in a strong updraught inside a cumulonimbus cloud and fall when they become too heavy

items: A hygrometer measures the humidity of the air, and a rain gauge measures the rainfall.
Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid water on a cold surface, and it is the same process that forms the dew on grass at night.
Clouds form when air rises, cools and reaches saturation; the main cloud types are cirrus, stratus, cumulus and cumulonimbus.
Heavy rain with thunder and lightning comes from cumulonimbus clouds, whose strong updraughts build the cloud high into the freezing layers.
Relative humidity of 100 per cent does not necessarily mean that rain will fall; the air must also be cooled further for the droplets to grow large enough to fall.

figures.caption: Figure: The layers of the atmosphere
figures.description: The troposphere contains all the weather and thins towards the poles. The stratosphere above it warms with height and holds the ozone layer. The mesosphere is the coldest layer and the scene of burning meteors. The thermosphere contains the ionosphere and the auroras, and the exosphere fades into space.

figures.caption: Figure: Pressure belts and wind systems
figures.description: Bands of high and low pressure alternate from the Equator to the poles: equatorial low at 0 degrees, subtropical high at about 30 degrees, subpolar low at about 60 degrees and polar high at 90 degrees. The trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies blow between them and are deflected by the rotation of the Earth.

keyPoints: Dry air is about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and other gases in trace amounts.
Water vapour makes up under 1 per cent of the air over the poles and about 4 per cent in warm humid air.
The atmosphere is denser at the Equator than at the poles and thins with height.
The troposphere extends 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the Equator, and holds all the weather.
Temperature falls about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre in the troposphere and rises with height in the stratosphere.
The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere and absorbs harmful ultra-violet radiation.
The mesosphere is the coldest layer and meteors burn up there.
Insolation depends on the angle of the rays and the length of the day, and the Equator receives more than the poles.
The greenhouse effect is caused by carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, which absorb the outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The pressure belts lie at the Equator, at about 30 degrees, at about 60 degrees and at the poles.
The trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies are the three wind systems, all deflected by the Coriolis force.
Wind is named after the direction it comes from.
Relative humidity reaches 100 per cent at the dew point, when condensation and cloud formation begin.
Rain, snow, sleet and hail are the four forms of precipitation.
examFocus: A layer-of-the-atmosphere question must give the height, the trend of temperature and the one special feature of each layer, so prepare a four-column table.
Insolation questions are usually set in pairs with the greenhouse effect; the first is about the incoming energy and the second about the outgoing energy, and the two must not be confused.
For the wind systems, say which belt each wind blows from and to, and give the direction of the deflection, because the deflection is what the question is usually testing.
A question on humidity expects the terms absolute humidity, relative humidity and dew point, and the definition of condensation.
For the forms of precipitation, the condition of the temperature between the cloud and the ground is what distinguishes one from another.

questions.prompt: The layer of the atmosphere in which all weather occurs is the:
questions.explanation: All weather takes place in the troposphere, the lowest layer, because it contains almost all the water vapour of the atmosphere. It extends to about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the Equator.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the stratosphere, which holds the ozone layer and is where aircraft fly.

questions.prompt: The ozone layer is found in the:
questions.explanation: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, roughly between 18 and 50 km above the surface, and it absorbs much of the harmful ultra-violet radiation from the Sun.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the troposphere, where the ozone that reaches the ground is found as pollution.

questions.explanation: Winds are named after the direction from which they blow, so a north-westerly wind comes from the north-west and travels towards the south-east.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 'towards the north-west', which reverses the convention and is a common trap.

options: Falls about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometre of height
Rises about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometre of height
questions.answer: Falls about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometre of height
questions.explanation: The troposphere is heated from below by the surface, so its temperature falls steadily with height at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre, and this is the normal lapse rate.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the rising rate, which is the behaviour of the stratosphere where ozone absorbs the radiation.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: dry air is made up of about 78 per cent ________ and 21 per cent oxygen.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of dry air by volume and oxygen about 21 per cent. The small remainder is argon, carbon dioxide and other gases in trace amounts.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'carbon dioxide', which is present in only trace amounts of about 0.04 per cent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the temperature at which the air becomes saturated and condensation begins is called the ________.
questions.explanation: At the dew point the relative humidity reaches 100 per cent, and any further cooling makes the excess water vapour condense, first as dew and then as cloud.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'condensation', which is the process rather than the temperature at which it starts.

questions.prompt: Explain why the troposphere is thicker at the Equator than at the poles.
questions.answer: The air of the troposphere is heated from below by the surface, and the Equator receives much more insolation than the poles, so the air above the Equator is much warmer. Warm air expands, and the expanded air is lighter, so the same weight of air occupies a greater height. The troposphere therefore extends to about 18 km at the Equator but only to about 8 km at the poles. The same expansion explains why the density of the atmosphere is greater at the poles than at the Equator.
questions.explanation: The chain is insolation, heating, expansion, greater height, and the thickness of the layer.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the atmosphere is thicker at the Equator because more air is piled up there, which reverses the weight argument.

questions.prompt: Explain the greenhouse effect and state why it is a problem today.
questions.answer: The Sun's short-wave radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface of the Earth. The warm surface then sends out long-wave heat energy, that is terrestrial radiation. Certain gases in the atmosphere, principally carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, absorb much of this outgoing radiation, and they send part of it back downwards, which warms the surface and the lower atmosphere. This is the natural greenhouse effect, and without it the Earth would be far too cold for life. It has become a problem because human activity has increased the concentration of these gases. The burning of coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide, the destruction of forests removes the vegetation that takes carbon dioxide out of the air, and the keeping of cattle and the decay of landfill waste add methane. The extra greenhouse effect is the main cause of the present warming of the globe, which brings heavier rainfall in some regions, droughts in others, the melting of glaciers, the rise of sea level and more frequent extremes of heat.
questions.explanation: The mechanism must be given first, and only then the human causes and the consequences.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the greenhouse effect is the same as global warming; the effect is natural and only its increase is a problem.

questions.prompt: Describe the wind systems of the world, naming the pressure belts and the winds that blow between them.
questions.answer: At the Equator, about 0 degrees, is the equatorial low pressure belt, also called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, where the trade winds of the two hemispheres converge and heavy rain falls. At about 30 degrees north and south is the subtropical high pressure belt, the horse latitudes, which is the source of both the trade winds and the westerlies. At about 60 degrees is the subpolar low pressure belt, the stormy belt, where the westerlies and the polar easterlies meet, and at the poles is the polar high pressure belt. The trade winds blow from the subtropical high towards the equatorial low, from the north-east in the Northern Hemisphere and from the south-east in the Southern Hemisphere. The westerlies blow from the subpolar low towards the subtropical high, from the south-west in the Northern Hemisphere and from the north-west in the Southern Hemisphere. The polar easterlies blow from the polar high towards the subpolar low. All these winds are deflected by the rotation of the Earth.
questions.explanation: The answer should pair each belt with the wind that blows away from it, and mention the deflection.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the winds without the pressure belts they blow from, which loses the structure of the question.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between rain, snow, sleet and hail.
questions.answer: All four are forms of precipitation, and they differ in the state of the water and in the process that produces them. Rain is liquid water falling from cloud as drops; it is the usual form in the tropics and in temperate countries in summer. Snow falls as ice crystals and reaches the ground as snow when the temperature of the air remains below freezing all the way from the cloud to the ground. Sleet is rain that passes through a shallow layer of freezing air near the ground and freezes into small pellets before reaching the surface. Hail is quite different: it forms inside a cumulonimbus cloud, where strong updraughts carry droplets of water repeatedly above the freezing level so that they freeze and grow into balls of ice, which fall when they become too heavy to be held up.
questions.explanation: The distinction turns on the temperature conditions for the last three and on the process inside the cloud for hail.
questions.commonMistake: Describing hail as frozen rain, when it grows in layers inside a thundercloud.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the atmosphere, giving for each layer its height, the behaviour of temperature and one important feature, and explain how the temperature pattern arises in each.
questions.answer: The atmosphere is divided into five layers. The troposphere extends from the surface to about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the Equator, and its temperature falls about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre with height. This is because the layer is heated from below by the surface, which the Sun has warmed, and the air loses heat as it rises and expands. The stratosphere extends from about 18 km to 50 km and its temperature rises with height, because ozone in the layer absorbs the ultra-violet radiation from the Sun and converts it into heat, and the warmed gas at the top of the layer prevents the heat from escaping. The mesosphere extends from about 50 km to 80 to 85 km, and its temperature falls with height to about minus 90 degrees Celsius at the mesopause, because there is very little ozone to absorb radiation and very little air left to be warmed. The thermosphere extends from about 80 km to about 500 km and beyond, and its temperature rises to very high values, because the few remaining atoms absorb the short-wave ultraviolet and X-ray radiation directly; the auroras occur in this layer. The exosphere lies above about 500 km, where the air is so thin that the temperature is very low and the atmosphere merges gradually into space. The height of the boundaries varies with latitude and with the season, because the temperature of the whole atmosphere changes through the year.
questions.explanation: Each layer is given with height, temperature trend and feature, and the reason for the temperature trend is stated separately.
questions.commonMistake: Listing the layers without explaining why the temperature rises in the stratosphere, which is the point most often tested.

questions.prompt: Examine how the rotation of the Earth shapes the pattern of winds and the pressure belts, and explain why the same belt gives opposite winds in the two hemispheres.
questions.answer: The heating of the Earth is uneven, because the Sun's rays strike directly at the Equator and obliquely towards the poles, so the Equator is hot and expands while the poles are cold and contract. The warm air of the Equator rises, leaving a low pressure area, and the cold air of the poles sinks, producing a high pressure area, with belts of high and low pressure between them at about 30 and 60 degrees. Air then flows from the high pressure belts towards the low pressure belts. The rotation of the Earth does not create the belts but it deflects the winds that flow between them, through the Coriolis force, which turns moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The trade winds are therefore north-easterly in the Northern Hemisphere, where the flow from the subtropical high is turned to the right, and south-easterly in the Southern Hemisphere, where the same flow is turned to the left. The westerlies are south-westerly in the Northern Hemisphere and north-westerly in the Southern Hemisphere, and the polar easterlies are north-easterly in the north and south-easterly in the south. The result is not a series of simple bands but a set of large circular systems, the gyres, in each ocean and hemisphere, and it is this pattern that carries heat from the equator towards the poles and shapes the climates of the coasts. The reason the belts give opposite winds in the two hemispheres is therefore that the starting flow is the same, from the high towards the low, but the deflection is reversed because the direction of the Earth's rotation is reversed when it is viewed from the opposite pole.
questions.explanation: The answer separates the cause of the belts from the cause of the deflection, and explains the reversal in terms of the rotation seen from the opposite pole.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the Coriolis force creates the pressure belts, when it only deflects the winds that flow between them.
